question: The EU’s Ecolabel criteria for growing media categorically state that a product may not contain intentionally added peat.1 However, a scientific article dating from 2026, with researchers from NIBIO, SLU and elsewhere, stresses that sustainability is not an inherent characteristic of an individual material, but must be assessed at system level and encompass environmental, economic and social consequences.
2 Therefore, the fact that a product is ‘peat‑free’ does not in itself show that its overall sustainability is better. In light of the above: 1.
What scientific basis justifies the categorical exclusion of peat from the EU Ecolabel, rather than it being assessed on the basis of actual life-cycle performance?
In light of new research, does the Commission intend to review the approach where ‘peat-free’ is used as an indirect indicator of sustainability?

Going forward, will the Commission distinguish more clearly between responsibly produced horticultural peat and energy peat, and take into account function, transport, resource consumption and the environmental impact of the alternatives?

Commission Decision (EU) 2022/1244 establishing the EU Ecolabel criteria for growing media and soil improvers, Annex, criterion 1, OJ L 190, 19.7.2022. 2 Aurdal et al., The challenge of defining ‘sustainable growing media’: why the term is used incorrectly and what needs to be done about it, doi: 10.3389/fhort.2026.1800902. 1
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.10.2026) The EU Ecolabel criteria1 are based on the best environmental performance of products available on the European Economic Area (EEA) market at the moment of their adoption. The criteria are developed and revised in consultation with key stakeholders, in accordance with Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 66/2010 on the EU Ecolabel2.

They are based on scientific data and information covering the entire life cycle of products. In the specific case of the EU Ecolabel criteria for growing media and soil improvers3, adopted in 2022, relevant information on the revision process can be found in the Final Technical Report on the revision of the EU Ecolabel criteria for growing media and soil improvers4.

This Report sets out the rationale for the exclusion of intentionally added peat as a component of the products, namely because ‘it affects valuable habitats for wildlife and contributes to the emission of sequestered carbon into the atmosphere, accelerating climate change’ (page 25 onwards for further information).

The EU Ecolabel criteria are revised periodically to ensure that they remain up to date, robust and reliable, while also taking account of technical innovation and market developments. Therefore, at the time of the next revision of the criteria for growing media and soil improvers, the most recent relevant scientific evidence and stakeholders’ views will be considered.
